target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for everyone
objection: A federal holiday would not, by itself, eliminate the practical time constraints that keep many people from voting, because U.S. labor law does not require private employers to give paid time off or close. Low-income workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs would often still have to work, so the holiday would not make voting easier for everyone and could even widen inequality in access.

target: AG2's assumption that because employers are not legally required to provide paid leave, a holiday would leave scheduling barriers essentially unchanged
objection: Even without legal compulsion, a federal holiday changes the default operating schedule: schools, public institutions, and many employers already align with holiday calendars, making closures, reduced staffing, and shift swaps more likely. That means the holiday would still reduce scheduling friction for millions of workers rather than leaving the status quo intact.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would directly remove the main turnout obstacle of time constraints
objection: Making Election Day a federal holiday would not reliably remove time constraints for the people most likely to have inflexible schedules, because many private employers would still operate and would not have to provide paid time off. Thus the holiday would be uneven in its benefits and would not be a dependable or equitable turnout solution.

target: AG2's premise that the holiday would not meaningfully change daily scheduling for workers because employers are not forced to close or pay
objection: A federal holiday typically changes real scheduling in practice: many workplaces close or reduce staffing, and many employers already offer paid holiday leave. So the holiday would give millions of workers usable time to vote and would not be merely symbolic.

target: AG1's claim that federal holiday designation would produce workplace closure and paid leave for millions of workers
objection: That outcome depends on employer behavior, not the calendar. Many retail, food service, and caregiving jobs can still operate on holidays, and hourly workers often do not automatically receive paid holiday leave, so the holiday would not reliably create the voting time the proposal assumes.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is just a calendar label and cannot change access in practice
objection: A federal holiday changes social meaning and coordination around the day: it increases civic salience, encourages workplace and community accommodations, and makes brief voting time windows easier to arrange. The policy can therefore improve practical access even without forcing every employer to close or pay.

target: AG1's argument that social meaning and coordination effects will make the holiday practically helpful for inflexible workers
objection: Changing how voting is talked about does not reliably change whether service-sector workplaces can spare employees. Supervisors still need coverage, shift swaps are constrained because everyone faces the same day-off decision, and workers without paid leave still risk lost wages, so the holiday does not reliably improve access for those most constrained by time.

target: AG2's assumption that federal-holiday status will not reliably change staffing and time-off decisions in practice
objection: That assumption overlooks how federal holidays usually alter scheduling: holiday calendars drive reduced operations, holiday coverage plans, and standard paid-leave practices. So the holiday can change day-to-day staffing and reduce scheduling friction even without legal compulsion.

target: AG1's claim that social meaning and holiday observance create a dependable pathway to voting time
objection: For hourly workers in sectors like retail, food service, and caregiving, holidays still require staffing and coverage. Supervisors cannot always accommodate time off, shift swaps are limited when everyone is trying to vote, and without paid leave the practical barrier remains, so the holiday does not reliably create voting time for the workers who most need it.

target: AG2's assumption that because there is no legal compulsion, hourly workers' scheduling reality will remain essentially unchanged
objection: Federal holidays often change staffing conditions in practice: many workplaces close or run reduced schedules, and many employers already treat federal holidays as paid time off. That means a holiday can reduce the coverage-vs-voting tradeoff and create real flexibility for hourly workers.

target: AG1's claim that social meaning effects make the holiday a dependable way to help workers with inflexible schedules
objection: A holiday may increase visibility, but it does not reliably let hourly workers be absent or take paid time. Holiday operations in service sectors still require staffing, supervisors cannot always accommodate absences, and the result is an uneven benefit that favors flexible workers while leaving low-income service workers' time barriers largely intact.

target: AG2's assumption that a lack of legal compulsion means the holiday will not change practical scheduling conditions
objection: That assumption treats legal compulsion as the whole mechanism. In reality, holiday status changes real operations because workplaces and schools plan around it, often with closures, reduced staffing, and shift coverage. Those changes can make it easier for workers to find time to vote.

target: AG1's claim that an Election Day holiday would directly reduce barriers and keep pressure for better reforms
objection: A holiday is likely to function as a substitute policy: it creates the appearance that access has been addressed, even though hourly and service workers still lack guaranteed paid time off or workplace closure. That false sense of solution can reduce pressure to adopt more effective reforms like required employer time off or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would function as a substitute that discourages stronger reforms
objection: The holiday can directly reduce scheduling barriers while leaving the access gap visible, so it does not replace the need for enforceable protections. Because it improves voting time for many people without fully solving the problem, it can complement rather than suppress additional reforms.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday is a good policy in its own right because it complements enforceable reforms
objection: A federal holiday is not a standalone access reform because it does not reliably give hourly, low-income workers actual time off or workplace closure. If policymakers rely on it, the key barrier remains; if they also pass enforceable reforms, those reforms do the real work and the holiday adds only limited marginal benefit.

target: AG2's premise that lack of enforceable paid time off means the holiday cannot reliably solve the time constraint
objection: That premise ignores how federal holidays work in practice: schools and many workplaces treat them as non-routine days, often with closures or reduced staffing. So the holiday can still provide predictable voting time for many workers, even without an enforceable right to paid leave.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday is a good standalone policy because it creates scheduling coordination and leaves gaps visible
objection: The holiday does not create an enforceable right to time off or closure, so it cannot consistently give the least flexible voters the actual time they need. Research-style comparisons also suggest holiday-only election policies are less effective at increasing turnout than direct access reforms such as required time off or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2's claim that without legal compulsion the holiday cannot provide predictable, operational time to vote
objection: Federal holiday status still changes day-to-day schedules because schools and many workplaces treat such days as non-routine, often closing or reducing operations. That creates predictable voting windows and reduces the time-friction that keeps people from voting.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would not mainly benefit already-advantaged voters and would complement reforms
objection: The holiday is likely to help voters who already have flexible schedules or paid leave, while leaving the time-off and wage-loss barrier largely intact for hourly, low-income workers. That persistence means the policy can look successful in aggregate while the most constrained workers remain underserved, making the holiday function politically like a substitute that reduces pressure for stronger reforms.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday mostly helps the advantaged and functions as a substitute policy
objection: A national holiday changes the baseline structure of the day for a broad range of workers, including hourly workers, because schools and many workplaces treat federal holidays as non-routine. And because the holiday does not make paid time off universal, the remaining gaps still leave room for enforceable reforms, so it complements rather than displaces them.

target: AG1's assumption that workplaces and schools commonly treat major federal holidays as non-routine in ways that help most hourly workers
objection: Federal holiday status is not enforceable time off. Private employers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar sectors often stay open and schedule staff as usual, so the holiday does not reliably create the universal workable time window needed for low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that federal holiday status merely creates calendar visibility and serves as a substitute for real reforms
objection: A holiday does more than provide symbolic visibility: it changes the baseline schedule because schools and many workplaces close, reduce hours, or use holiday staffing, giving many workers real time to vote. The remaining gaps stay visible, so the holiday need not reduce pressure for enforceable reforms.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday creates a different baseline schedule that solves the time constraint for many workers
objection: The holiday does not remove the operational problem for many low-income workers, because private employers are not required to close or provide paid time off. Service jobs commonly remain open on holidays, so many workers still have to work or lose wages, leaving the core time constraint intact.

target: AG2's claim that federal holiday status is mostly calendar visibility and that the operational barrier remains largely intact
objection: A national holiday changes the practical structure of the day for many workers and students by making it non-routine and reducing scheduling pressure. That creates predictable time windows to vote and can materially reduce the barrier even without universal legal compulsion.
